title: Laser Micromachining Research at MTF STU Trnava — Overview of 7 Diploma Theses

slides.title: Title — Laser Micromachining Research at MTF STU Trnava
slides.narration: This presentation provides an overview of seven diploma theses on laser micromachining conducted at the Institute of Production Technologies, Faculty of Materials Science and Technology, Slovak University of Technology in Trnava. The research spans the years 2013 to 2018 and covers three distinct application areas of laser technology.

slides.title: Research Overview — Three Categories
slides.narration: The seven theses are grouped into three categories. Category A focuses on laser parameter optimisation — finding the best settings for machining specific materials. Category B examines laser surface texturing to modify tribological properties, measured through Ring test experiments. Category C covers applied manufacturing — using the laser to produce actual functional parts. The common experimental platform across all studies is the DMG MORI LASERTEC 80 Shape, a five-axis CNC laser machining centre located at the Centre of Excellence for Five-Axis Machining at MTF STU Trnava.

slides.title: A1: Titanium Alloy GRADE 2 — Experiment Design
slides.narration: The first parameter optimisation study investigated laser micromachining of commercially pure titanium alloy GRADE 2. The experiment used a Taguchi L9 orthogonal matrix with four factors — pulse frequency, power, scan speed, and track spacing — each tested at three levels, resulting in nine machining runs. Two scanning strategies were compared: hatching, where the laser moves in one direction, and cross-hatching, where it moves in two perpendicular directions. Surface roughness Ra was measured in two perpendicular directions to assess isotropy.

slides.title: A1: Taguchi L9 — Factors and Scanning Strategies
slides.narration: The four process parameters were varied across three levels each. Pulse frequency ranged from 40 to 80 kilohertz, laser power from 50 to 100 percent, scan speed from 1000 to 2200 millimetres per second, and track spacing from 5 to 15 micrometres. The hatching strategy produces parallel scan lines in a single direction, while cross-hatching overlays two perpendicular sets of lines. This difference in strategy significantly affects both surface quality and its directional uniformity.

slides.title: A1: Results — Surface Roughness Ra
slides.narration: The best surface roughness achieved with hatching was 1.17 micrometres Ra, obtained at 80 kilohertz, 75 percent power, 1000 millimetres per second, and 15 micrometre track spacing. However, the same surface measured perpendicularly showed Ra of 2.26 micrometres — highly anisotropic. Cross-hatching yielded 1.55 and 1.57 micrometres in both directions at 60 kilohertz, 50 percent power, 1600 millimetres per second, and 15 micrometre spacing. This isotropy makes cross-hatching preferable for practical applications. In all experiments, track spacing had the greatest influence on Ra, exceeding 50 percent, while scan speed had the least effect.

slides.title: A2: Sintered Carbide WC-Co — Experiment Design
slides.narration: The second parameter optimisation study focused on sintered carbide — one of the hardest cutting tool materials. The samples were uncoated turning inserts from Pramet, containing 10 percent cobalt and the remainder tungsten carbide. A half-factorial design with 27 experiments was used, testing the same four factors at three levels. Based on findings from the titanium study, only cross-hatching was used here. Two output metrics were measured: surface roughness Ra and ablation rate — the volume of material removed per unit time.

slides.title: A2: Sintered Carbide — Machined Surface Comparison
slides.narration: These microscope images show the sintered carbide surfaces after laser machining under different parameter combinations. Visible differences in surface texture, groove regularity, and re-solidified material can be observed across experiments. The study confirmed that track spacing and laser power are the most influential parameters for both surface quality and material removal rate on sintered carbide with this machine. The results provide a practical calibration baseline for laser machining of this specific material on the LASERTEC 80 Shape.

slides.title: Ring Test Method — Shared Methodology for Category B
slides.narration: All three Category B studies use the Ring test to measure friction. In this test, a metal ring is compressed between two tool surfaces. Because the inner diameter is sensitive to friction at the contact interface, changes in inner diameter after each compression step are used to determine the friction coefficient from a calibration curve. A lower friction surface causes the inner diameter to increase, while higher friction causes it to decrease. The test was conducted on a hydraulic EU 40 press in the forming technology laboratory at MTF STU Trnava.

slides.title: B1: Steel 11373 — Three Structure Types
slides.narration: The first tribological study created three types of microstructures on steel ring samples. Type A consisted of narrow parallel grooves machined by a commercial marking laser. Type B was wide, deep grooves produced on the LASERTEC 80 Shape. Type C was hemispherical dimples, also made on the LASERTEC 80 Shape, with diameter approximately 0.15 millimetres and two different pitch angles. A reference sample with no surface structuring served as the friction baseline.

slides.title: B1: Steel 11373 — Ring Test Results
slides.narration: The reference smooth surface gave a friction coefficient of 0.189. Narrow groove samples showed increased friction, between 0.22 and 0.26, because melt ridges along the groove edges raised effective surface roughness. The wide groove sample B1 achieved the lowest friction of 0.128 — a 32 percent reduction — because the large groove geometry created minimal real contact area. Hemisphere-textured samples had friction close to the reference. The study recommends that future work include lubrication testing, as structured surfaces acting as lubricant reservoirs may show even greater friction reduction.

slides.title: B2: Tool Steel 1.2311 — Large Triangular Microstructures
slides.narration: The second tribological study machined a triangular grid microstructure onto the face of tool steel compression rings using the LASERTEC 80 PowerDrill. Each triangular element had arm lengths of 500 micrometres and cavity depth of approximately 410 micrometres. Due to manufacturing limitations, the design had been scaled up ten times from the original 50-micrometre concept. Machining one experimental sample took approximately nine hours. Surface quality was verified by microscopy before ring test.

slides.title: B2: Tool Steel 1.2311 — Unexpected Friction Increase
slides.narration: Contrary to expectations, the microstructured surface increased friction from 0.258 to 0.315 — a 22 percent rise. The root cause was the excessive structure size: during ring compression, metal material flowed into the deep triangular cavities, creating additional resistance. This finding reframes the application: these large structures are not suitable for friction reduction but are appropriate for surfaces where increased grip is desirable, such as robot clamping jaws or anti-slip contact faces. The recommendation is to return to the original 50-micrometre design using a femtosecond laser for adequate precision.

slides.title: B3: Tool Steel 90MnCrV8 — 4 Textures and 3 Lubricants
slides.narration: The third tribological study applied four different paraboloid dimple texture designs to the face of compression tool punches made from tool steel 90MnCrV8. The LASERTEC 80 Shape was used for texturing. Three lubrication conditions were tested in the Ring test: dry contact, low-viscosity cutting fluid Variocut C462, and high-viscosity forming oil Iloform FST4. This systematic approach allowed separating the effects of texture geometry from lubricant properties.

slides.title: B3: Tool Steel 90MnCrV8 — Results Table
slides.narration: The results show that the most effective combination was Texture IV with Variocut C462, achieving a friction coefficient of 0.158 — a 46 percent reduction compared to the smooth reference. In dry conditions, only Texture I showed significant reduction to 0.183. With the high-viscosity Iloform FST4, lubrication effects dominated and the textures provided no measurable benefit. An important manufacturing limitation was discovered: the 10-micrometre deep textures could not be produced to the required quality on the LASERTEC 80 Shape, which suggests that pico- or femtosecond lasers would be better suited for such fine dimple geometries.

slides.title: C1: Chip Breaker on Cutting Insert — Workflow
slides.narration: The first applied manufacturing study aimed to design and produce a chip breaker geometry on a sintered carbide turning insert using laser — as an alternative to conventional grinding. The workflow began with CAD design in Autodesk Inventor, followed by CAM programming in LpsWin software to generate the laser paths from an STL file. Machining was performed on the LASERTEC 80 Shape with a track spacing of 10 micrometres and 1-micrometre material removal per layer. Six parameter tests identified the optimal settings as 60 kilohertz, 2000 millimetres per second, and approximately 29 watts.

slides.title: C1: Chip Breaker — 3D Scan Verification Results
slides.narration: The produced chip breaker was verified by 3D optical scanning using an ATOS GOM scanner. The colour deviation map shows the geometric difference between the machined surface and the original CAD model — red areas are above the design, blue areas below. The maximum deviation measured was 0.09 millimetres. While the chip breaker shape was correctly reproduced, this deviation is too large for serial production standards. Machining one side of an insert took 25 to 30 minutes, confirming that this approach is most valuable for prototype development and geometry exploration during the R&D phase of new cutting tool designs.

slides.title: C2: Injection Mold Texturing — Workflow
slides.narration: The second applied manufacturing study transferred decorative and functional laser textures to plastic injection-moulded parts. The workflow involved designing four texture geometries in Autodesk PowerSHAPE, converting them to bitmap images, and applying them to the mold cavity surface using GIMP graphic software. The LpsWin software generated laser paths for the LASERTEC 80 Shape at a track spacing of 20 micrometres and 2-micrometre material removal per layer. Plastic parts were then produced by injection moulding using HDPE material on a Babyplast micro-injection machine.

slides.title: C2: Injection Mold Texturing — Results
slides.narration: The first round of texturing failed because the 0.4 to 0.84 millimetre textures were too small to transfer visibly to plastic parts. After redesigning to 4 millimetre dimensions, two of four textures met requirements, though a jetting effect from poor gate design and an oval mold artifact persisted. Five-axis texturing of a complex 3D cavity surface was successfully performed, though texture quality degraded near the cavity centre — possibly due to programming error or fixture movement during machining. The hexagonal texture performed best due to its greater depth. The key engineering conclusion is that texture depth exceeding 1 millimetre is critical for reliable visual transfer to the plastic part.

slides.title: Summary — 7 Research Theses
slides.narration: This table summarises the seven theses across the three research categories. Category A established optimal laser parameters for titanium and sintered carbide, identifying track spacing as the most influential factor. Category B showed that laser surface texturing can reduce friction by up to 46 percent when the texture geometry and lubricant viscosity are properly matched, and revealed that oversized structures unexpectedly increase friction — a valuable finding for grip applications. Category C demonstrated that laser micromachining is a viable tool for prototype chip breaker production and for creating functional mold surface textures transferable to plastic parts. All seven studies utilised the LASERTEC 80 Shape at the Centre of Excellence for Five-Axis Machining at MTF STU Trnava.
